newsitem.title: USA: Bond lawyers must play safe on disclosure - SEC.
newsitem.headline: Bond lawyers must play safe on disclosure - SEC.

text.p: A top SEC enforcement official urged municipalities and their lawyers Thursday to play it safe when deciding whether to disclose a new piece of information to investors about a municipality's finances.

"Why would you even want to take a chance?" Colleen Mahoney, deputy director of enforcement at the Securities and Exchange Commission, told a workshop at the National Association of Bond Lawyers annual workshop here on Thursday.
"If you are wringing your hands, I would think you'd want to err on the side of disclosure rather than non-disclosure," Mahoney said.
She added, "It is always better to make the tough call than to try to play it cute."
Mahoney was responding to a workshop participant who asked what is the worst thing that can happen to an issuer if it incorrectly opts not to disclose information.
Mahoney also was asked whether SEC's enforcement staff makes allowances for the fact that many municipalities do not have the same internal accounting controls as corporations to detect fraud.
"It's not a yes or no answer," Mahoney said. "We recognize that some issuers are operating in a difficult context."
"A bad system may explain why the information was not what it needed to be," she said. But an important question, she said, is whether local officials were reckless in not knowing about system flaws.

Earlier today, Dean Pope, a partner with Hunton & Williams in Richmond, told lawyers that many of their early fears about the new provisions of SEC's municipal disclosure Rule 15c2-12 were "exaggerated."

He said issuers generally are pledging to make only those disclosures specifically required by the rule. "This approach, I believe, is indisputably correct, and is in the best interest of your clients," Pope said in a keynote address at the NABL conference.
Pope said once bonds hit the secondary market, disclosing ongoing events about the issuer "continues to be the great unknown."
"Few of our clients have had much experience with it," he said.

Pope turned to SEC's probe of Denver International Airport bonds. To what extent should bond professionals rely on forecasts in financings for airports, hospitals, retirement communities, and utility systems? Pope asked.

"Is every risk that is ever raised in project planning a risk that must be" disclosed, Pope asked. "How relevant is the fact that, despite large shifts in market value, the bonds have never defaulted?"
He said Denver is a reminder that for high profile, political projects there is an "inherent tension" between providing investors with bad news and "glowing" reports.

On May 2, an SEC administrative law judge ruled that Thorn, Welch & Co., formerly Thorn, Alvis, Welch Inc, failed to tell investors in seven tax-exempt bond deals that the deals were structured so as to violate tax laws and threaten the tax status of the bonds.
Judge Brenda Murray revoked the firm's broker-dealer registration and ordered it and its president John Thorn to pay over $1 million in fines.

Pope said, "I believe that when we are wearing the hat of bond counsel, Thorn Alvis doesn't change what we do at all. We still apply the standards that we have been taught to apply in giving opinions," he said.

SEC in January 1995 filed its first "pay-to-play" case against Terry Busbee, an elected official of the Escambia county, Florida, Utilities Authority, and Preston Bynum, who worked for bond underwriter Stephens Inc.
Both defendants agreed to settle the charges.
Pope said the case reflects SEC's "not terribly convincing" position that "any kind of political bribe in connection with retention of underwriters is a material event to be disclosed."
"Guilty pleas meant this assertion was not judicially tested," he said.
He said there is "substantial doubt" as to whether the SEC can prevail with this position in futures cases.
--Vicky Stamas, 202-898-8314
